title: (Scenario) A Kafka partition reassignment is triggered for scaling/rebalancing and you observe spikes in consumer lag and latency — explain the five causes: (1) data copying saturates disk I/O and network on source/destination brokers, (2) throttling slows replication but keeps the pipe busy longer, (3) leader movement causes consumers to reconnect (NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors + metadata refresh), (4) cold page cache on the new broker forces disk reads instead of memory reads until cache warms, (5) coordination overhead from ISR changes and metadata propagation — and why you should monitor replication throughput, avoid reassignment during peak traffic, and throttle appropriately?
shortTitle: (Scenario) A partition reassignment for scaling/rebalancing causes spikes in consumer lag and latency — explain the five causes and how to mitigate them.

s1_definition.profdef: A partition reassignment moves partition replicas from one set of brokers to another, which Kafka does to rebalance load, add or drain brokers, or recover from failures. Although it is an online operation, it causes transient consumer lag and latency spikes for five reasons: bulk data copying saturates disk and network on the source and destination brokers, replication throttling reduces the rate but extends the duration of contention, leader movement forces producers and consumers to reconnect and refresh metadata after NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors, the destination broker's page cache is cold so reads hit disk until it warms, and the coordination overhead of in-sync replica changes and metadata propagation adds churn. Mitigation is to monitor replication throughput, avoid reassignment during peak traffic, and apply appropriate throttles.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India is relocating the records for some accounts from one branch vault to another while the branch stays open. Moving boxes of ledgers ties up the loading dock and the delivery trucks, so normal deliveries slow down; that is disk and network saturation. To avoid blocking the dock completely, the movers go slower, but then the trucks occupy the dock for longer; that is throttling trading rate for duration. While an account's master ledger is being moved, tellers who try to use the old vault are told "that ledger moved, go to the new vault," and they have to look up the new location; that is leader movement and metadata refresh. At the new vault, the clerks have not memorized where anything is yet, so every lookup means walking to the shelves instead of recalling from memory; that is a cold cache. And the branch manager has to keep updating the master directory of which vault holds what, which itself takes effort; that is coordination overhead.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reassignment copies data online, so lag spikes come from disk and network saturation, throttling that trades rate for duration, leader moves that force metadata refresh, cold page cache on the destination, and coordination churn — mitigate by monitoring replication throughput, avoiding peak hours, and throttling appropriately.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A partition reassignment moves partition replicas from one set of brokers to another, which Kafka does to rebalance load, add or drain brokers, or recover from failures. Although it is an online operation, it causes transient consumer lag and latency spikes for five reasons: bulk data copying saturates disk and network on the source and destination brokers, replication throttling reduces the rate but extends the duration of contention, leader movement forces producers and consumers to reconnect and refresh metadata after NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION errors, the destination broker's page cache is cold so reads hit disk until it warms, and the coordination overhead of in-sync replica changes and metadata propagation adds churn. Mitigation is to monitor replication throughput, avoid reassignment during peak traffic, and apply appropriate throttles.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India is relocating the records for some accounts from one branch vault to another while the branch stays open. Moving boxes of ledgers ties up the loading dock and the delivery trucks, so normal deliveries slow down; that is disk and network saturation. To avoid blocking the dock completely, the movers go slower, but then the trucks occupy the dock for longer; that is throttling trading rate for duration. While an account's master ledger is being moved, tellers who try to use the old vault are told "that ledger moved, go to the new vault," and they have to look up the new location; that is leader movement and metadata refresh. At the new vault, the clerks have not memorized where anything is yet, so every lookup means walking to the shelves instead of recalling from memory; that is a cold cache. And the branch manager has to keep updating the master directory of which vault holds what, which itself takes effort; that is coordination overhead.

**One line to remember:** Reassignment copies data online, so lag spikes come from disk and network saturation, throttling that trades rate for duration, leader moves that force metadata refresh, cold page cache on the destination, and coordination churn — mitigate by monitoring replication throughput, avoiding peak hours, and throttling appropriately.

sections.s2_technical:
Cause one is bulk data copying saturating disk and network. When a replica is reassigned to a new broker, that broker must fetch the entire partition log from the leader, which can be gigabytes. This replication competes with normal produce and consume traffic for the same disks and network links on both the source and destination brokers. Since consuming often reads from the page cache and produce writes sequentially, suddenly adding large sequential reads for replication and large writes for the new replica steals I/O bandwidth, slowing the foreground traffic and causing lag to rise.

Cause two is throttling that keeps the pipe busy longer. To protect foreground traffic you apply a replication throttle, which caps the bytes per second used for moving data. This genuinely reduces the instantaneous contention, which is good, but it also extends how long the reassignment runs. So instead of a short, sharp spike you get a longer, gentler elevation of lag. The lesson is that throttling is a trade between intensity and duration, and you must size it so the reassignment still finishes in a reasonable window rather than dragging on for hours while catching up is impossible.

Cause three is leader movement forcing reconnection and metadata refresh. Reassignment often changes which broker is the leader for a partition. When the leader moves, producers and consumers that were talking to the old leader get a NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION error, must refresh cluster metadata to discover the new leader, and reconnect. During that brief window, requests for the affected partitions fail and retry, which shows up as a latency spike and a momentary lag bump. Clients handle this automatically, but at scale many partitions moving at once can cause a burst of metadata refreshes across the fleet.

Cause four is the cold page cache on the destination broker. Kafka relies heavily on the operating system page cache so that consumers reading recent data are served from memory, not disk. A broker that just received a replica has none of that partition's data in its page cache, so once it becomes leader, consumer fetches for that partition initially miss the cache and hit disk, which is far slower. Latency for that partition stays elevated until enough data is read and the cache warms. This is why a partition can be fully in-sync yet still slow right after a move.

Cause five is coordination overhead. Every replica movement changes the in-sync replica set, which the controller must track, and the resulting metadata updates must propagate to all brokers and clients. In-sync replica shrink and expansion events, leader elections, and metadata epoch bumps all add bookkeeping that momentarily competes with serving traffic, especially when many partitions are reassigned simultaneously. Individually small, these add up into measurable churn during a large reassignment.

The three mitigations map onto these causes. You monitor replication throughput and the partition reassignment progress so you can see whether you are saturating links or falling behind, using broker metrics for replication bytes and the reassignment tool's verify mode. You avoid reassignment during peak traffic, scheduling it for low-traffic windows so the extra I/O and the cold-cache period overlap with spare capacity rather than competing with your busiest load. And you throttle appropriately, setting leader and follower replication rate limits high enough to finish in a reasonable time but low enough to protect foreground traffic, and you move partitions in small batches rather than all at once to bound leader movement, metadata churn, and the number of simultaneously cold replicas. Here is how you drive it:

```bash
# Generate and execute a reassignment plan, then verify progress.
kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file plan.json --execute \
  --throttle 50000000   # 50 MB/s cap on replication to protect foreground traffic

kafka-reassign-partitions.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 \
  --reassignment-json-file plan.json --verify   # removes throttle when complete
```

Senior-level nuances: prefer moving a few partitions at a time so only a small fraction of clients see NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION at once; pre-warm or accept a warm-up window for the destination before relying on it as leader by delaying the preferred-leader election until the new replica has caught up and served some reads; set the throttle dynamically and raise it near the end when the cluster is calmer; and always run verify to ensure the throttle configuration is cleaned up, because a forgotten throttle silently caps replication forever and causes mysterious under-replication later.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India added two new brokers to the cluster and ran a partition reassignment to balance load onto them. During the move, the settlement consumer group showed sharp lag spikes and elevated end-to-end latency, alarming the on-call team. Rajesh and Priya transfers flow through this cluster.

Problem 1 — the reassignment copied several large partitions at full speed with no throttle, saturating disk and network on the source and destination brokers, so foreground consume slowed and lag jumped. This is causes one and two: raw copying contention, and the realization that we needed a throttle, which then trades rate for duration.

Problem 2 — as leaders moved to the new brokers, settlement consumers briefly got NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refreshed metadata, reconnected, and then hit a cold page cache on the new brokers, so even after catching up, latency stayed high for a while. This is causes three, four, and five: leader movement and metadata refresh, cold cache, and coordination churn.

Our runnable demo models a `ReassignmentPlan`, a `Broker` with disk and network budgets and a page cache warmth level, and a `ReassignmentSimulator` that runs the move with and without throttling and in peak versus off-peak windows, reporting the lag spike magnitude and duration. The classes are `ReassignmentDemo`, `Broker`, `Partition`, `ReassignmentPlan`, and `ReassignmentSimulator`.

Configuration file:

```yaml
# application.yml
ops:
  reassignment:
    throttle-bytes-per-sec: 50000000     # 50 MB/s replication cap
    batch-size: 4                        # move at most 4 partitions at a time
    allowed-window: "02:00-05:00"        # off-peak only
cluster:
  bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four large settlement partitions being reassigned to new brokers, run first unthrottled at peak and then throttled off-peak.

Step 1: The reassignment starts copying each partition's full log from the source leader to the destination broker. Unthrottled, this copying runs at full speed and consumes most of the disk and network bandwidth on both brokers, leaving little headroom for foreground consume. Lag begins to rise. This is cause one.

Step 2: We add a fifty megabyte per second throttle. Contention drops because replication no longer hogs the links, but the total copy now takes longer, so the elevated lag persists for a longer, gentler window instead of a short, sharp spike. This is cause two, the rate-versus-duration trade.

Step 3: As each partition's leader moves to a new broker, settlement consumers talking to the old leader receive NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refresh cluster metadata, find the new leader, and reconnect. Requests for those partitions briefly fail and retry, producing a latency bump. This is cause three.

Step 4: Immediately after a leader moves, the destination broker's page cache holds none of that partition's data, so consumer fetches miss the cache and read from disk, keeping latency high until the cache warms through repeated reads. This is cause four, and it explains why a partition can be in-sync yet still slow.

Step 5: Throughout, the controller tracks in-sync replica changes and propagates metadata updates across the cluster, which is extra bookkeeping competing with serving traffic, amplified when many partitions move at once. This is cause five. In the off-peak throttled batched run, all five effects overlap with spare capacity and are moved a few partitions at a time, so the lag stays contained and recovers quickly.

Final output:

```
[2026-10-25 00:20:14] [INFO] === Unthrottled, during PEAK traffic (bad) ===
[2026-10-25 00:20:14] [SEVERE] LAG SPIKE=4060 msgs over 40s | contention=380MB/s leaderMoves=4 coldCacheMs=50 churn=12
[2026-10-25 00:20:14] [INFO] Note: throttle lowers contention but increases duration (40s) — trade rate for duration
[2026-10-25 00:20:14] [INFO] === Throttled 50 MB/s, OFF-PEAK, small batches (good) ===
```

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Partition reassignment: move settle-0..3 to new brokers (online)
    │
    ├─ CAUSE 1: bulk copy log (GBs) source->dest : saturates disk + network
    ├─ CAUSE 2: throttle reduces rate BUT extends duration (rate vs time trade)
    ├─ CAUSE 3: leader moves -> clients get NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION
    │             -> metadata refresh + reconnect -> latency bump
    ├─ CAUSE 4: dest page cache COLD -> fetches hit disk until warm
    ├─ CAUSE 5: ISR changes + metadata propagation -> coordination churn
    ▼
  CONSUMER LAG + LATENCY SPIKE (transient)
    │
    ├─ MITIGATE: monitor replication throughput (bytes/s, reassign verify)
    ├─ MITIGATE: run OFF-PEAK (spare I/O absorbs the move + cold cache window)
    └─ MITIGATE: throttle appropriately + small batches (bound leader moves/churn)
    ▼
  contained, fast-recovering lag
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A partition reassignment is an online operation that moves replicas between brokers for scaling, rebalancing, or recovery, and even though clients stay up, it causes transient consumer lag and latency spikes for five distinct reasons. First, the destination broker must copy the entire partition log, often gigabytes, from the source, and that bulk transfer saturates disk and network on both brokers, stealing I/O from normal consume and produce. Second, if you add a replication throttle to protect foreground traffic, it genuinely lowers the instantaneous contention but extends how long the move runs, so you trade a short sharp spike for a longer gentle one. Third, when leaders move to the new brokers, producers and consumers hit NOT_LEADER_FOR_PARTITION, refresh cluster metadata, and reconnect, which causes a brief failure-and-retry latency bump. Fourth, the destination broker's page cache is cold, so right after it becomes leader, consumer fetches miss memory and hit disk until the cache warms, keeping that partition slow even once it is in-sync. Fifth, every move changes the in-sync replica set and triggers metadata propagation, and that coordination overhead adds churn, especially when many partitions move at once.

On the National Bank of India cluster we saw exactly this when we added brokers and reassigned partitions onto them. Running unthrottled during peak hours, the copy saturated the links and settlement lag jumped, and as leaders moved, consumers briefly got not-leader errors, refreshed metadata, and then hit cold caches on the new brokers, so latency stayed elevated for a while even after catching up.

The three mitigations map directly onto those causes. I monitor replication throughput and the reassignment progress so I can see whether I am saturating links or falling behind, using the broker replication byte metrics and the reassignment tool's verify mode. I avoid reassignment during peak traffic and schedule it for a low-traffic window, so the extra I/O and the cold-cache warm-up period overlap with spare capacity instead of competing with the busiest load. And I throttle appropriately, setting the replication rate limit high enough to finish in a reasonable time but low enough to protect foreground traffic, while moving partitions in small batches rather than all at once so that only a few clients see not-leader errors at any moment and only a few replicas are cold simultaneously.

The senior details I always add are to delay promoting a freshly moved replica to leader until it has caught up and warmed a little, to raise the throttle near the end when the cluster is calmer, and to always run verify so the throttle configuration is removed afterward, because a forgotten throttle silently caps replication forever and causes mysterious under-replication later. The mental model is that reassignment is safe and online, but it is real work on finite disk, network, cache, and coordination resources, so you plan it like any capacity-sensitive operation rather than firing it off at full speed during your busiest hour.
